subject: biology

items.q: A biologist collects an organism from a deep-sea vent that has never been examined before. Before looking at it under a microscope, she predicts that it will consist of one or more cells. Which statement best describes this reasoning?
items.correct: It is deductive: a specific prediction is derived from cell theory, and examining the organism then tests it.
items.misconception: It is inductive: the prediction is a generalization drawn from the many organisms already examined.
items.why: Students meet induction first, as 'science is based on observation', and the word 'deduce' is used loosely in everyday speech to mean any kind of working-out. Because cell theory was itself built up inductively from observations, students attach the word 'inductive' to anything that involves the theory. Induction moves from many particular observations to a general statement, which is how cell theory was established. Deduction moves the other way, from a general theory to a particular prediction: if all organisms are made of cells, then this new organism will be made of cells. Using cell theory to predict the structure of an unexamined organism is deductive reasoning, and the prediction is tested by examining the organism.
items.specStatementText: All living organisms are made of cells, so new ones can be predicted to be
items.random_wrong: It is unscientific: cell theory cannot be relied on until every living organism has been examined.

items.q: In a photomicrograph taken at a magnification of ×2000, a red blood cell measures 15 mm across. What is the actual width of the cell?
items.correct: 7.5 µm
items.why: Students remember that magnification makes things bigger and so multiply by it, instead of rearranging magnification = image size ÷ actual size to make actual size the subject. Magnification = size of image ÷ actual size, so actual size = size of image ÷ magnification. Multiplying instead gives an 'actual' cell larger than the image, which is impossible for a magnified image. Conversely, the length of a scale bar or the size of an image is found by multiplying the actual size by the magnification.
items.specStatementText: Using a light microscope and calculating size

items.q: With the ×40 objective lens in place, 40 divisions of an eyepiece graticule line up exactly with 100 µm on a stage micrometer. Using the same objective, a cell spans 44 graticule divisions. What is the actual length of the cell in millimetres?
items.why: Rulers have fixed divisions, and the graticule looks like a ruler laid on the specimen. Students do not realize that the graticule sits in the eyepiece, above the objective, so changing the objective changes how much of the specimen lies under each division. The graticule is a scale of arbitrary divisions in the eyepiece. When the objective is changed, the specimen is magnified by a different amount but the graticule is not, so each division corresponds to a different actual length. The graticule is calibrated by lining it up with a stage micrometer under each objective; the number of divisions spanned by a specimen is then multiplied by the calibrated value for that objective.
items.specStatementText: Using a light microscope and calculating size

items.q: A student makes a drawing of a cell at a magnification of ×1250 and wants to add a scale bar representing 10 µm. How long should the scale bar be drawn?
items.misconception: 125 mm
items.why: The prefixes milli- and micro- are learned together and both refer to 'very small', and students rarely handle the factor of 1000 between them until magnification calculations force them to. 1 mm = 1000 µm and 1 µm = 1000 nm. In a magnification calculation both lengths must be in the same unit; a mismatch or a slip in the power of ten produces answers that are 10, 100 or 1000 times too large or too small. A check on plausibility helps: a typical animal cell is tens of micrometres across, a bacterium a few micrometres.
items.specStatementText: Using a light microscope and calculating size

items.q: A student focuses a stained temporary mount at low power, then rotates the high-power objective lens into place. The image is now slightly blurred. What should the student do?
items.correct: Turn only the fine adjustment until the image is sharp.
items.misconception: Turn the coarse adjustment, since it changes the focus most quickly.
items.why: The names suggest that coarse is for big problems and fine is for small ones, and at low power the coarse adjustment is what students have used successfully to find the specimen. At high power the objective lens is very close to the slide and the depth of focus is very small. The coarse adjustment moves the lens by large amounts, so it overshoots the focus and can drive the lens into the slide, breaking the slide or damaging the lens. The specimen is focused with the coarse adjustment at low power, then the high-power objective is rotated into place and only the fine adjustment is used.
items.specStatementText: Using a light microscope and calculating size
items.random_wrong: Add more stain to the mount so the structures show up clearly.

items.q: Ribosomes are about 25 nm across. They cannot be seen with a light microscope but are clearly visible in electron micrographs. What is the reason?
items.correct: Electrons have a far shorter wavelength than light, so the resolution is much higher.
items.misconception: The electron microscope magnifies many more times, so much smaller objects become visible.
items.why: Magnification is the quantity students calculate and see written on micrographs, so it is the familiar idea. Resolution is not calculated at this level and is easily left out of the explanation. Resolution, the smallest distance at which two points can be told apart, is limited by the wavelength of the radiation used. Light limits a light microscope to about 200 nm; an electron beam has a far shorter wavelength, giving an electron microscope a resolution below 1 nm. Above the resolution limit, further magnification produces a larger image but no more detail, so the advantage of electron microscopy is its resolution, which makes its high magnifications useful.
items.specStatementText: Newer microscopy techniques and what each one gains
items.random_wrong: Heavy-metal stains used for electron microscopy make small structures much sharper.

items.q: In freeze fracture, a rapidly frozen cell is split with a blade, the exposed surface is coated with metal, and the replica is examined by electron microscopy. Replicas of plasma membranes show a smooth face scattered with small bumps. What does this show?
items.correct: The fracture ran between the two phospholipid layers, and the bumps are proteins embedded within the bilayer.
items.misconception: The fracture cut straight across the cell, and the bumps are organelles seen in cross-section.
items.why: Students picture fracturing as cutting with a knife, and every micrograph they have seen is a section. That a fracture follows the weakest plane, which lies inside a membrane, is counter-intuitive. A frozen membrane breaks most easily along the plane where the hydrophobic tails of the two phospholipid layers meet, because there are no strong bonds across it. The fracture therefore splits membranes into their two layers and exposes their interior faces. Proteins embedded in the bilayer are left standing as particles on one face, which is why freeze fracture gave evidence that proteins are embedded within membranes rather than lying on their surfaces.
items.specStatementText: Newer microscopy techniques and what each one gains
items.random_wrong: Ice crystals grew inside the membrane as it froze, and the bumps are the crystals left in the replica.

items.q: A researcher wants to see where one particular protein is located inside cultured cells. Which approach will show this?
items.correct: Immunofluorescence: antibodies that bind only that protein carry a fluorescent marker seen with a light microscope.
items.misconception: A general stain such as methylene blue, which binds to proteins so that every location of the protein is coloured.
items.why: The stains students have used themselves (iodine, methylene blue) colour broad classes of material, so 'stain' comes to mean something that colours the whole cell. The specificity of antibodies is not part of most students' experience of microscopy. A fluorescent stain glows against a dark background and can be chosen to bind to a particular component, such as DNA. In immunofluorescence the fluorescent marker is attached to an antibody, and an antibody binds only to one specific protein. The glow therefore appears only where that protein is, which shows the distribution of a single type of protein in the cell. Different antibodies with different coloured markers can show several proteins at once.
items.specStatementText: Newer microscopy techniques and what each one gains
items.random_wrong: A higher-power objective lens, since enough magnification will show which structures contain the protein.

items.q: What is the main advantage of cryogenic electron microscopy over conventional electron microscopy?
items.correct: Rapid freezing keeps unfixed, unstained molecules near their natural state, so structures are resolved in near-atomic detail.
items.misconception: Heavy-metal stains bind more firmly at very low temperature, so the contrast between structures in the specimen is much greater.
items.why: Students know from frozen food and from cell biology that ice crystals damage cells, and the name 'cryogenic' suggests only that the microscope is cold; they are not told that the point is the speed of freezing. Ice crystals form when water freezes slowly. In cryogenic electron microscopy the specimen is plunged into a very cold liquid so that the water solidifies in a fraction of a second into a glass-like solid with no crystals. Because no fixation or staining is needed, proteins and other molecules are seen in their natural shape, and combining images of many identical molecules gives three-dimensional structures at near-atomic resolution.
items.specStatementText: Newer microscopy techniques and what each one gains
items.random_wrong: Freezing makes the cell brittle, so it can be fractured to reveal the interior of its membranes in section.

items.q: Every living cell has DNA as genetic material, a cytoplasm composed mainly of water, and a plasma membrane composed of lipids. Which statement gives a correct reason for one of these features?
items.correct: The membrane is made of lipids because their hydrophobic tails form a barrier to the water-soluble contents of the cell.
items.misconception: The cytoplasm is mainly water so that it forms a stiff gel that holds every organelle in a fixed position.
items.why: Cytoplasm is described in earlier courses as 'jelly-like', and students see organelles drawn in fixed positions in diagrams, so they picture a solid gel rather than a solution. Cytoplasm is about 70–80% water, with proteins and other solutes dissolved or suspended in it. Water is required because metabolism consists of reactions between dissolved substances, catalysed by enzymes in solution, and because substances move through the cell by diffusion in water. Organelles are not held rigidly; they move, and the cytoskeleton, not the cytoplasm's consistency, positions them.
items.specStatementText: What every cell has, and why
items.random_wrong: The membrane is made of lipids because lipids form a rigid layer that gives the cell its strength and shape.

items.q: Which description of the structure of a Bacillus cell is correct?
items.correct: A loop of naked DNA lies in the cytoplasm, and proteins are made on 70S ribosomes.
items.misconception: The DNA is enclosed by a nuclear membrane inside a small nucleus within the cytoplasm.
items.why: Plant and animal cells are met first, and the nucleus is their most obvious feature, so it becomes part of the definition of a cell. Diagrams of bacteria often show the DNA as a dark region that looks like a nucleus. The structures common to all cells are DNA as genetic material, a cytoplasm composed mainly of water and a plasma membrane composed of lipids. A nucleus is not one of them: prokaryotes have their DNA in a nucleoid region of the cytoplasm, not enclosed by a membrane. Some eukaryotic cells, such as mature red blood cells, have also lost their nucleus.
items.specStatementText: Prokaryotic cell structure
items.random_wrong: The cell wall outside the plasma membrane is built from long parallel fibres of cellulose.

items.q: A unicellular organism is found to have a cell wall, a plasma membrane and ribosomes, but no nucleus. Its DNA is a single circular molecule, not associated with histones, lying in the cytoplasm. A student concludes that the organism is a prokaryote. Which evaluation of this conclusion is correct?
items.correct: It is justified: naked circular DNA in the cytoplasm with no nucleus is a prokaryotic feature.
items.misconception: It is wrong: the presence of a cell wall means the organism must be either a plant or a fungus.
items.why: The GCSE and MYP comparison of animal and plant cells lists the cell wall as the plant feature, and the wall is the first thing students look for when classifying a cell. A cell wall is present in plant cells, fungal cells and prokaryotic cells, so on its own it only rules out an animal cell. To classify a cell in a micrograph, look at the DNA: a nucleoid region with no membrane and no membrane-bound organelles indicates a prokaryote. A nucleus with a cell wall and a large sap vacuole or chloroplasts indicates a plant cell; a nucleus with no cell wall indicates an animal cell.
items.specStatementText: Prokaryotic cell structure
items.random_wrong: It is wrong: prokaryotes are too simple to have ribosomes, so this must be a eukaryote.

items.q: Which statement about the structure of a eukaryotic cell is correct?
items.correct: The nucleus is bounded by a double membrane with pores, and its DNA is bound to histone proteins.
items.misconception: The nucleus is enclosed by a single membrane that is continuous with the plasma membrane.
items.why: Diagrams at GCSE and MYP level draw every organelle as a single outline, and the plasma membrane, the only membrane discussed in detail, is a single bilayer. The nucleus is enclosed by a double membrane, the nuclear envelope, perforated by nuclear pores through which RNA and proteins pass. Mitochondria and chloroplasts are also bounded by double membranes. Lysosomes, vesicles, the endoplasmic reticulum and the Golgi apparatus are bounded by single membranes. The number of membranes is visible in electron micrographs and is used to identify organelles.
items.specStatementText: Eukaryotic cell structure
items.random_wrong: The ribosomes in the cytoplasm are 70S, the same size as those found in bacteria.

items.q: Which statement correctly describes a membrane-bound organelle of a eukaryotic cell?
items.correct: Lysosomes are vesicles bounded by a single membrane that contain hydrolytic enzymes.
items.misconception: The Golgi apparatus is a stack of flattened sacs studded with ribosomes that synthesize proteins.
items.why: The Golgi apparatus is always described as part of the pathway for secreted proteins, and its stacked sacs look like the rough endoplasmic reticulum in diagrams, so students merge the two organelles and give the Golgi the better-known function. Protein synthesis takes place only on ribosomes. Proteins for secretion are made on ribosomes attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum, transported to the Golgi apparatus in vesicles, then modified (for example by adding carbohydrate), sorted and packaged into secretory vesicles. The Golgi apparatus has no ribosomes on its surface, which is one way to tell it from rough endoplasmic reticulum in an electron micrograph.
items.specStatementText: Eukaryotic cell structure
items.random_wrong: Mitochondria are bounded by a single membrane folded inward to form cristae.

items.q: Paramecium is a unicellular organism that lives in fresh water. Which statement correctly identifies one of its functions of life?
items.correct: Homeostasis: expelling water that enters by osmosis, keeping the water content of the cytoplasm within limits.
items.misconception: Growth: dividing by binary fission, so that the single cell becomes two separate cells.
items.why: Cell division is introduced as the way multicellular organisms grow, and 'reproduction' in everyday language means sexual reproduction with two parents. In a unicellular organism the cell is the whole organism, so when it divides into two, two organisms exist where there was one, and that is reproduction (asexual reproduction). Growth in a unicellular organism is the increase in size of the single cell between divisions.
items.specStatementText: One cell can carry out every function of life
items.random_wrong: Excretion: a process not carried out, because removing metabolic waste requires organs such as kidneys.

items.q: Which row correctly compares the cells of animals, fungi and plants?
items.correct: Cell wall: absent in animals, made of chitin in fungi, made of cellulose in plants.
items.misconception: Cell wall: absent in animals, made of cellulose in fungi, made of cellulose in plants.
items.why: Fungi were classified as plants until the twentieth century, mushrooms grow from the ground and do not move, and fungal cells have a cell wall, so students group them with plants. Fungi form a separate kingdom. Fungal cells have a cell wall, but it is made of chitin, the same polymer found in insect exoskeletons, not cellulose. They have no chloroplasts or other plastids and cannot photosynthesize; they secrete enzymes and absorb the products. The presence and composition of the cell wall and the presence of plastids are among the features that distinguish animal, fungal and plant cells.
items.specStatementText: How animal, fungal and plant cells differ
items.random_wrong: Vacuoles: absent in animals, present in fungi, present as a large sap vacuole in plants.

items.q: A cell taken from a multicellular organism has a cell wall, a nucleus, no chloroplasts and no centrioles. A student concludes that it must be a fungal cell. Is this conclusion justified?
items.correct: No: a plant root cell also fits every feature listed, and the composition of the wall would decide between them.
items.misconception: Yes: every plant cell contains chloroplasts, so the absence of chloroplasts rules out a plant cell.
items.why: The plant cell in almost every diagram is a leaf cell packed with chloroplasts, so chloroplasts become a defining feature of plant cells rather than a feature of photosynthetic plant cells. Chloroplasts are present in plant cells but not in every plant cell: root cells, cells in the interior of stems and storage tissues have none, and they may contain other plastids such as amyloplasts that store starch. The reliable distinguishing features of a plant cell are the cellulose cell wall and the large sap vacuole; the absence of chloroplasts does not rule out a plant cell.
items.specStatementText: How animal, fungal and plant cells differ
items.random_wrong: No: fungal and plant cell walls are both made of cellulose, so the composition of the wall cannot help to decide either.

items.q: Which statement correctly describes the number of nuclei in an atypical eukaryotic cell?
items.correct: An aseptate fungal hypha contains many nuclei within one continuous cytoplasm.
items.misconception: A mature red blood cell keeps a single nucleus so that it can control the making of haemoglobin.
items.why: Red blood cells are drawn as simple discs and the absence of a nucleus is easy to miss; students also reason that a cell full of protein must be making it, which needs a nucleus. A mature mammalian red blood cell has no nucleus. The haemoglobin was made while the developing cell still had a nucleus and ribosomes; the nucleus is then expelled, which increases the space available for haemoglobin and allows the cell's biconcave shape. Without a nucleus the cell cannot make new proteins or divide, so red blood cells last only about 120 days and are continually replaced.
items.specStatementText: Cells that break the one-nucleus rule
items.random_wrong: A skeletal muscle fibre has a single, very large nucleus to control its whole length.

items.q: An electron micrograph shows a cell about 3 µm long. It has a cell wall, a paler fibrous region of DNA not enclosed by any membrane, many small dense granules, and no membrane-bound organelles. How should the cell be classified?
items.correct: As a prokaryote, because its DNA lies in a nucleoid region and it has no membrane-bound organelles.
items.misconception: As a eukaryote, because prokaryotic cells are too simple to contain any ribosomes.
items.why: Prokaryotes are introduced as cells that 'lack organelles', and ribosomes are listed among the 'organelles' of eukaryotic cells, so students remove them along with the mitochondria and nucleus. Every living cell makes proteins, so every living cell has ribosomes. Prokaryotes lack membrane-bound organelles, and ribosomes are not membrane-bound, so their presence is consistent with prokaryotic structure. Prokaryotic ribosomes are 70S, smaller than the 80S ribosomes of the eukaryotic cytoplasm.
items.specStatementText: Recognizing cell types and organelles in micrographs
items.random_wrong: As a plant cell, because a cell wall is found only around the cells of plants.

items.q: In an electron micrograph of an animal cell, a structure appears as a discrete stack of curved, flattened membrane sacs with small vesicles budding from its edges and no ribosomes attached. Which structure is it?
items.correct: Golgi apparatus, where proteins are modified and packaged
items.misconception: Smooth endoplasmic reticulum, where lipids are made
items.why: In diagrams the Golgi apparatus and the endoplasmic reticulum both look like stacks of sacs, and the rough/smooth distinction is the only difference between membrane sacs that students have been taught to look for. Smooth endoplasmic reticulum is a network of tubules without ribosomes, not a stack of flattened sacs. The Golgi apparatus is a separate stack of curved cisternae, not continuous with the nuclear envelope, with vesicles budding from its edges; it has no ribosomes on its surface. Rough endoplasmic reticulum is an extensive network of flattened sacs with ribosomes attached. Shape, position and budding vesicles, as well as ribosomes, identify each structure.
items.specStatementText: Recognizing cell types and organelles in micrographs
items.random_wrong: Mitochondrion, where aerobic cell respiration is carried out

items.q: A student draws a cell from an electron micrograph of a gland that secretes enzymes, and must annotate each structure with its function. Which annotation is correct?
items.correct: Rough endoplasmic reticulum — synthesizes proteins that are destined for secretion from the cell.
items.misconception: Microvilli — beat rhythmically to move the secreted enzymes along the surface of the cell.
items.why: Cilia and microvilli are both hair-like projections from the cell surface, and 'villi' is met in the context of the small intestine where movement of food is also discussed. Microvilli are finger-like extensions of the plasma membrane supported by microfilaments; they do not move and contain no microtubules. Their function is to increase the surface area for absorption, for example in cells lining the small intestine. Cilia are longer, contain microtubules, and beat to move the cell or move fluid past it.
items.specStatementText: Drawing and annotating cell structures from micrographs
items.random_wrong: Golgi apparatus — synthesizes the enzymes that the cell will later secrete by exocytosis.

items.q: If mitochondria originated as free-living prokaryotes taken into a larger cell, which features would the theory of endosymbiosis predict mitochondria to have?
items.correct: Naked circular DNA and 70S ribosomes, with the ability to divide independently of the host cell.
items.misconception: Ribosomes identical to those of the cytoplasm, because the host cell now makes them all.
items.why: Ribosomes are introduced as 'the site of protein synthesis' with no mention of size, and their function is the same everywhere, so students assume the structure is the same too. Prokaryotes have 70S ribosomes; the cytoplasm of eukaryotes has larger 80S ribosomes. (HL) The ribosomes inside mitochondria and chloroplasts are 70S, like those of prokaryotes, which is one line of evidence that these organelles evolved from prokaryotes by endosymbiosis. The difference also matters medically, because some antibiotics act on 70S but not 80S ribosomes.
items.specStatementText: Mitochondria and chloroplasts were once free-living prokaryotes
items.random_wrong: DNA wound around histone proteins, because all DNA in the cell is packaged in that way.

items.q: Evidence suggests that all eukaryotes evolved from a common unicellular ancestor that had a nucleus, that mitochondria then evolved by endosymbiosis, and that in some eukaryotes chloroplasts subsequently also had an endosymbiotic origin. Which conclusion is consistent with this evidence and with the nature of scientific theories?
items.correct: The ancestors of plants already had mitochondria when a photosynthetic prokaryote was taken in as a chloroplast.
items.misconception: The earliest eukaryotes were photosynthetic, and lineages such as animals and fungi have since lost their chloroplasts.
items.why: Plants are thought of as 'simpler' and 'earlier' than animals, and food chains start with producers, so students assume photosynthetic organisms came first at every level. Mitochondria are found in essentially all eukaryotes, whereas chloroplasts are found only in plants and algae, which is what is expected if mitochondria were acquired in the common ancestor of all eukaryotes and chloroplasts were acquired later in one lineage. There is no evidence that animals or fungi ever had chloroplasts. Photosynthesis itself is older than eukaryotes, but it was carried out by prokaryotes, one of which became the chloroplast.
items.specStatementText: Mitochondria and chloroplasts were once free-living prokaryotes
items.random_wrong: The nucleus itself arose when an early cell engulfed a prokaryote, in the same way as mitochondria arose.

items.q: A muscle cell and a neurone from the same person contain the same genome, yet they differ greatly in structure and function. What is the basis of this difference?
items.correct: Different sets of genes are expressed in each cell, often triggered by its environment.
items.misconception: Each cell has kept only the genes it needs and has lost the genes for the other cell type.
items.why: The permanence of differentiation in most animal cells suggests that something has been lost, and 'the cell no longer has the gene' is a simpler explanation than gene expression. All the differentiated cells of a multicellular organism, with very few exceptions, contain the same complete genome as the zygote. Differentiation is a change in which genes are expressed, not in which genes are present: a muscle cell expresses genes for contractile proteins and keeps the genes for neurone proteins switched off. This is why a nucleus from a differentiated cell can be used to produce a whole organism by cloning.
items.specStatementText: Cells specialize by expressing different genes
items.random_wrong: Each cell's fate was fixed at fertilization by its genes alone, with no influence from its surroundings.

items.q: Which statement about the evolution of multicellularity is correct?
items.correct: Multicellularity evolved independently in several eukaryotic lineages, including plants, animals and fungi.
items.misconception: Multicellularity evolved only once, so all multicellular organisms descend from a single multicellular ancestor.
items.why: Major features such as the nucleus or mitochondria are taught as having arisen once in a common ancestor, and evolutionary trees show multicellular kingdoms as branches from one trunk. The closest relatives of plants, of animals and of fungi are unicellular, which shows that each of these groups became multicellular separately. Multicellularity is also found in several groups of algae that are not closely related to one another. Because it evolved repeatedly, its advantages, larger body size and cell specialization, must have been available in many lineages.
items.specStatementText: Multicellularity evolved many times and brings two advantages
items.random_wrong: Unicellular eukaryotes are transitional forms that will become multicellular given enough time.

items.q: Are viruses an exception to cell theory?
items.correct: No. Viruses are not cells and are not considered to be living organisms, so cell theory, which applies to living organisms, is not contradicted by them.
items.misconception: Viruses are living organisms that are not made of cells, so cell theory has exceptions.
items.why: Viruses are described as 'infecting', 'reproducing' and 'evolving', which are things living organisms do, and they are treated alongside bacteria as 'germs' or 'microbes' in earlier courses, so students file them as very small living things. Cell theory states that living organisms consist of one or more cells. Viruses have no cytoplasm, no metabolism of their own and cannot reproduce outside a host cell, so they are not classified as living organisms and are not exceptions to the theory. A prediction from cell theory that a newly discovered organism will consist of cells is not undermined by the existence of viruses.
items.specStatementText: All living organisms are made of cells, so new ones can be predicted to be
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can a scientific theory be used to make a reliable prediction before every case has been observed?
items.correct: Yes. A theory that is supported by a wide range of observations can be used deductively to predict new cases, and testing those predictions is how the theory is further tested.
items.misconception: A theory is only a guess until every possible case has been observed, so it cannot be relied on to predict anything.
items.why: In everyday speech 'theory' means an unproven idea ('it's only a theory'), and students learn that science demands evidence, so they conclude that a theory has no standing until it has been confirmed in every instance. A scientific theory is a well-supported general explanation. Its value lies precisely in generating predictions about cases that have not yet been examined; the prediction is then tested and either supports the theory or reveals a problem with it. Cell theory can never be checked against every organism, but it has been tested against every organism examined so far and is used to predict the structure of new ones.
items.specStatementText: All living organisms are made of cells, so new ones can be predicted to be
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A drawing is made at ×2000. How long should a scale bar representing 10 µm be?
items.correct: 20 mm, because the scale bar is drawn at the actual length multiplied by the magnification: 10 µm × 2000 = 20 000 µm = 20 mm.
items.misconception: The number on a scale bar's label is the length to draw it, so a bar labelled 10 µm is drawn 10 mm (1 cm) long whatever the magnification.
items.why: The label states an actual length, and students take its number as an instruction for the length of the line in whatever unit is convenient on paper, rather than as the length in the specimen that the line stands for; they do not connect the drawn length to the magnification. A scale bar represents an actual length in the specimen, and it is drawn on an image that has been magnified, so its drawn length is the actual length multiplied by the magnification. A 10 µm bar on a ×2000 image is 20 mm long. The drawn length depends on the magnification, not on the number in the label: at ×1000 the same 10 µm bar would be 10 mm long, at ×2000 it is 20 mm.
items.specStatementText: Using a light microscope and calculating size
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why are stains used when making temporary mounts of cells?
items.correct: To increase contrast: most cell structures are almost transparent, and a stain that binds to particular components makes them visible against their surroundings.
items.misconception: Stains make the image sharper or larger, so a blurred image can be improved by adding more stain.
items.why: Stained specimens look much clearer than unstained ones, and students attribute the whole improvement to the stain without separating contrast from focus or resolution. A stain only adds contrast by colouring particular structures; it has no effect on magnification, which depends on the lenses, or on resolution, which depends on the wavelength of light. A blurred image at high power is corrected with the fine adjustment, and detail that is below the resolution of the light microscope cannot be revealed by any stain.
items.specStatementText: Using a light microscope and calculating size
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can living cells be observed with an electron microscope?
items.correct: No. Specimens must be fixed, dehydrated, usually stained with heavy metals, and placed in a vacuum, so they are dead; living cells are observed with light microscopy.
items.misconception: Electron microscopes can be used to watch living cells, and their images show the natural colours of cell structures.
items.why: Electron micrographs are often published with false colour added, and students see the electron microscope as simply a better microscope, assuming it can do everything a light microscope does at higher power. An electron beam travels only in a vacuum and is scattered by water, so the specimen must be dead, dehydrated and fixed, and it is usually stained with heavy metals to scatter electrons. Electrons carry no colour information, so the images are greyscale; any colour is added afterwards. Observing living cells and processes is an advantage of light microscopy, including fluorescence microscopy, over electron microscopy.
items.specStatementText: Newer microscopy techniques and what each one gains
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why is the plasma membrane composed of lipids?
items.correct: Because phospholipids have hydrophobic tails that form a bilayer barrier to water-soluble substances, separating the cell contents from the surroundings and controlling what enters and leaves.
items.misconception: The plasma membrane is a rigid layer, coated with protein, that holds the cell in shape like a wall.
items.why: 'Membrane' and 'wall' are both boundaries drawn as a line around the cell, and in animal cells the membrane is the only boundary, so students give it the supporting role of a wall. The plasma membrane is a flexible phospholipid bilayer with proteins embedded in it, not a rigid coat. Lipids are used because their hydrophobic tails exclude water and water-soluble substances, forming a barrier that keeps the aqueous cytoplasm separate from the outside; it is fluid, not stiff. Support and shape come from a cell wall, where present, and from the cytoskeleton.
items.specStatementText: What every cell has, and why

items.q: What is the cell wall of a bacterium such as Bacillus made of?
items.correct: Peptidoglycan; it is not made of cellulose.
items.misconception: All cell walls are made of cellulose, so a bacterial cell wall is a cellulose cell wall.
items.why: Students learn 'cell wall made of cellulose' for plant cells and then meet 'cell wall' in bacteria, assuming that the same name means the same material. Only plant cells have cellulose cell walls. The cell wall of a Gram-positive bacterium such as Bacillus or Staphylococcus is made of a thick layer of peptidoglycan, and fungal cell walls are made of chitin. The name 'cell wall' describes the position and function of the structure, not its composition.

items.q: What does 'naked' mean when prokaryotic DNA is described as naked?
items.correct: That the DNA is not associated with histone proteins. It also happens to lie in the cytoplasm without a nuclear membrane, but 'naked' refers to the absence of histones.
items.misconception: Naked DNA means DNA that is not enclosed by a membrane; the DNA itself is packaged with histone proteins in every cell.
items.why: The most obvious difference between a prokaryote and a eukaryote is the missing nuclear membrane, so students attach 'naked' to that. Histones are met later, in the context of eukaryotic chromosomes, and are assumed to be universal. Eukaryotic chromosomes consist of DNA bound to histone proteins. Prokaryotic DNA is a loop that is not bound to histones, which is what 'naked' means. The DNA also lies free in the nucleoid region of the cytoplasm rather than in a nucleus, but that is a separate feature. (HL) Mitochondria and chloroplasts also contain naked circular DNA, which is evidence of their prokaryotic origin.

items.q: What is the cytoskeleton like?
items.correct: A dynamic network of protein fibres, microtubules and microfilaments, that assemble and disassemble to change cell shape, move organelles and vesicles and separate chromosomes.
items.misconception: The cytoskeleton is a rigid, permanent frame of rods, like the bones of a skeleton, that holds each organelle in a fixed position.
items.why: The word 'skeleton' brings to mind a fixed frame of bones, and organelles are drawn in fixed positions in every cell diagram. Microtubules (tubulin) and microfilaments (actin) are constantly built up and broken down. They give the cell shape and mechanical support, but they also move: they transport vesicles and organelles, form the spindle that separates chromosomes during division, drive changes in cell shape and power the beating of cilia and flagella. The cytoskeleton is more like scaffolding that is continually rebuilt than like a bony skeleton.

items.q: Can a single-celled organism carry out homeostasis and excretion?
items.correct: Yes. All the functions of life, including homeostasis and excretion, are carried out within the one cell of a unicellular organism.
items.misconception: Processes such as homeostasis and excretion require organs such as kidneys, so a single cell cannot carry them out; unicellular organisms only feed, move and divide.
items.why: At GCSE and MYP level homeostasis and excretion are taught through the human body: kidneys, skin, sweating, the pancreas. Students attach the process to the organ rather than to the cell. A unicellular organism is a complete organism and must carry out every function of life within one cell: homeostasis (for example, a contractile vacuole keeps the water content of the cytoplasm within limits), metabolism, nutrition, movement, excretion (waste products of metabolism such as carbon dioxide diffuse out across the plasma membrane), growth, response to stimuli and reproduction. Organs are one way of carrying out these functions in a large multicellular body, not a requirement for them.

items.q: A contractile vacuole expels water that entered a Paramecium by osmosis. Is this excretion?
items.correct: No. It is homeostasis (osmoregulation), because the water is not a waste product of metabolism. Excretion is the removal of the waste products of metabolism, such as carbon dioxide.
items.misconception: Anything expelled from a cell is excretion, so expelling water from a contractile vacuole is excretion.
items.why: In everyday use 'excrete' means to get rid of anything, and students see the vacuole 'emptying' and match it to the only life process on the list that mentions removal. Excretion is defined as the removal of the waste products of metabolism. The water expelled by a contractile vacuole entered the cell by osmosis from the surroundings; it was not produced by the cell's metabolism. Expelling it keeps the water content of the cytoplasm within limits and prevents the cell bursting, which is homeostasis. The metabolic waste of a Paramecium, such as carbon dioxide, leaves by diffusion across the plasma membrane, and that is excretion.

items.q: What is metabolism?
items.correct: The sum of all the enzyme-catalysed reactions in an organism, including both the synthesis of molecules (anabolism) and their breakdown (catabolism).
items.misconception: Metabolism is the breaking down of food to release energy, so it means the same as respiration or the rate at which an organism burns calories.
items.why: In everyday speech 'metabolism' refers to how fast a person burns energy or loses weight, and respiration is the metabolic process students know best. Metabolism includes every chemical reaction the cell carries out: respiration and other breakdown reactions, but also the synthesis of proteins, lipids, nucleic acids and other molecules. A unicellular organism carries out both kinds of reaction in its one cell. Respiration is one part of metabolism, and the 'rate of metabolism' is a rate, not the process itself.

items.q: Do animal cells have vacuoles?
items.correct: Yes, but small and temporary ones, such as the vesicles formed when material is taken in by endocytosis; plant cells have a single large permanent sap vacuole.
items.misconception: Animal cells have no vacuoles at all; vacuoles are found only in plant cells.
items.why: The comparison table learned at GCSE and MYP level lists 'permanent vacuole' as a plant-only feature, and students drop the word 'permanent' and remember 'vacuole: plants only'. The difference between animal and plant cells is in the size and function of their vacuoles, not in whether they have them. Plant cells have a large permanent vacuole filled with cell sap that stores substances and maintains turgor. Animal cells contain small temporary vacuoles, formed for example when a cell takes in material by endocytosis, and these are among the variety of vesicles found in eukaryotic cells.

items.q: Do plant cells have centrioles?
items.correct: No. Plant cells lack centrioles but still form a spindle of microtubules during cell division; centrioles are found in animal cells.
items.misconception: Plant cells must have centrioles, because they divide by mitosis and the spindle is made by centrioles.
items.why: Mitosis is taught with animal cell diagrams in which centrioles sit at the spindle poles, so students conclude that no spindle can form without them. Centrioles are a feature of animal cells and are absent from plant cells. Microtubules of the spindle are organized in plant cells without centrioles, so mitosis and cytokinesis proceed normally. The presence of centrioles, and of cilia and flagella, is one of the differences between animal cells and the cells of plants and fungi.

items.q: Does every eukaryotic cell contain exactly one nucleus?
items.correct: No. Typical eukaryotic cells have one nucleus, but atypical cells exist: aseptate fungal hyphae and skeletal muscle fibres contain many nuclei, and mature red blood cells and phloem sieve tube elements have none.
items.misconception: Every eukaryotic cell has exactly one nucleus, because the nucleus is what defines a eukaryotic cell.
items.why: 'One nucleus per cell' is true of every cell students have drawn, and eukaryotes are defined by having a nucleus, so both a missing nucleus and multiple nuclei seem impossible. Eukaryotes are defined by the possession of membrane-bound organelles and, typically, a nucleus, but the number of nuclei in a cell can vary. Aseptate hyphae contain many nuclei because nuclei divide without the cytoplasm dividing; skeletal muscle fibres contain many nuclei because they form by the fusion of many cells; mature mammalian red blood cells and phloem sieve tube elements lose their nucleus during development.
items.specStatementText: Cells that break the one-nucleus rule

items.q: Is a phloem sieve tube element a living cell?
items.correct: Yes. It loses its nucleus and most organelles as it matures, but it retains cytoplasm and a plasma membrane and is kept alive by its companion cell.
items.misconception: Sieve tube elements are dead, hollow cells like xylem vessels, so they have no nucleus because they have no cytoplasm at all.
items.why: Xylem and phloem are taught together as transport tissues, and xylem vessels are dead hollow tubes, so students apply the same description to phloem. Phloem sieve tube elements are alive: they have a plasma membrane and cytoplasm, and transport in phloem depends on living cells. What is atypical is that a mature sieve tube element has no nucleus, having lost it during development, together with most of its organelles, so that sap can flow through the cell. An adjacent companion cell, which keeps its nucleus, supplies the sieve tube element with the proteins and ATP it needs.

items.q: How is a mitochondrion distinguished from a chloroplast in an electron micrograph?
items.correct: A mitochondrion has an inner membrane folded into cristae projecting into the matrix; a chloroplast contains separate stacks of flattened thylakoids (grana) and is usually much larger.
items.misconception: Any organelle with folded membranes inside it is a mitochondrion, so a structure showing internal membranes can be labelled as a mitochondrion without looking further.
items.why: The mitochondrion is the internal-membrane organelle students learn first and see most often, and cristae and grana are both 'membranes inside an organelle' in diagrams. Both mitochondria and chloroplasts have a double outer membrane and internal membranes, but they differ. Cristae are folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane, continuous with it. Thylakoids are separate flattened sacs stacked into grana within the chloroplast stroma, and the chloroplast is typically several times larger than a mitochondrion. The Golgi apparatus and endoplasmic reticulum are also membrane structures but have no enclosing double membrane.
items.specStatementText: Recognizing cell types and organelles in micrographs
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What makes rough endoplasmic reticulum 'rough'?
items.correct: Ribosomes attached to the outer surface of its membranes, which appear as dense granules in an electron micrograph.
items.misconception: 'Rough' describes the wrinkled, folded appearance of the membranes themselves, so any convoluted stack of membrane sacs in a micrograph can be labelled rough endoplasmic reticulum.
items.why: The names rough and smooth are learned before students see electron micrographs, and 'rough' is taken literally as a description of membrane texture; ribosomes are too small to feature in the mental picture of the organelle. 'Rough' refers to the ribosomes bound to the cytoplasmic face of the endoplasmic reticulum, visible as many small dense granules along the membranes, not to any folding or curvature of the membranes themselves. Vesicles bud from the rough endoplasmic reticulum, but budding vesicles at the edges of a stack of sacs without ribosomes are the characteristic appearance of the Golgi apparatus.

items.q: What is in a secretory vesicle?
items.correct: Proteins or other products made by the cell that are carried to the plasma membrane and released outside the cell by exocytosis.
items.misconception: All small vesicles are lysosomes, so a secretory vesicle contains hydrolytic enzymes that digest worn-out organelles.
items.why: Lysosomes are the vesicles with the most memorable function, and in micrographs one small membrane-bound sac looks much like another. Eukaryotic cells contain a variety of vesicles with different contents and functions. Secretory vesicles bud from the Golgi apparatus, carry products such as enzymes or hormones to the plasma membrane and release them from the cell by exocytosis. Lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes and act inside the cell. In an annotated drawing of a secretory cell, the vesicles between the Golgi apparatus and the plasma membrane are secretory vesicles, annotated with transport to the membrane and release of their contents.

items.q: Did the nucleus of eukaryotic cells arise by endosymbiosis?
items.correct: No. The evidence suggests that the common ancestor of eukaryotes already had a nucleus before mitochondria were acquired by endosymbiosis; the nucleus is not thought to be a former prokaryote.
items.misconception: The nucleus arose by endosymbiosis, when an early cell engulfed a prokaryote that became the nucleus, just as other engulfed prokaryotes became mitochondria and chloroplasts.
items.why: Once students learn that organelles can originate as engulfed cells, and see that the nucleus, like a mitochondrion, has a double membrane, they extend the explanation to every double-membraned structure. Endosymbiosis is the accepted explanation for mitochondria and chloroplasts, which have their own naked circular DNA, 70S ribosomes and the ability to replicate independently. The nucleus has none of these: its DNA is the cell's own, bound to histones, it has no ribosomes of its own and it does not divide independently, and its double membrane is continuous with the endoplasmic reticulum. The common ancestor of eukaryotes had a nucleus before it acquired mitochondria.
items.specStatementText: Mitochondria and chloroplasts were once free-living prokaryotes

items.q: Is endosymbiosis a weak theory because nobody observed the original engulfing events?
items.correct: No. The strength of a theory comes from the range of observations it explains and the predictions it supports, and endosymbiosis accounts for a wide range of observations about mitochondria and chloroplasts.
items.misconception: Because the endosymbiotic events happened over a billion years ago and were never observed, endosymbiosis is 'just a theory' and cannot be regarded as well supported.
items.why: In everyday speech 'theory' means a speculation, and students are taught that science depends on observation, so an unobservable past event seems to leave the theory without evidence. Scientific theories about the past are tested through their consequences in the present. Endosymbiosis explains why mitochondria and chloroplasts have naked circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, double membranes and the ability to replicate by dividing, why they resemble prokaryotes in size, and why their genes are more similar to bacterial genes than to those of the nucleus. It also predicted that some organelle genes would have been transferred to the nucleus, which has been confirmed. A theory that explains many observations and makes successful predictions is strong, whether or not the original event was witnessed.

items.q: Where did the two membranes of a mitochondrion come from?
items.correct: The inner membrane is derived from the plasma membrane of the engulfed prokaryote; the outer membrane is derived from the membrane of the vesicle in which the host cell enclosed it.
items.misconception: Both membranes of a mitochondrion came from the host cell, which wrapped the engulfed cell in two layers of membrane.
items.why: Students learn that endocytosis wraps a particle in host membrane, and picture the engulfed bacterium as a particle with no membrane of its own, so both layers are assigned to the host. The engulfed prokaryote had its own plasma membrane, and this became the inner mitochondrial membrane, which is folded into cristae and carries the proteins of aerobic respiration, as the bacterial membrane did. The host cell took the prokaryote in by endocytosis, and the vesicle membrane became the outer membrane. The double membrane with these different origins is one of the observations that endosymbiosis explains.

items.q: Is the fate of a cell fixed by its genes alone?
items.correct: No. Differentiation is based on different patterns of gene expression, and these are often triggered by changes in the cell's environment, such as signals from neighbouring cells or its position in the embryo.
items.misconception: A cell's type is determined entirely by its genes at fertilization, so the environment around a cell has no influence on what it becomes.
items.why: Students learn that genes determine characteristics, and all the cells of an organism share the same genes, so the environment appears to have no role at the level of a single cell. Because every cell has the same genes, something other than the genome must decide which genes each cell expresses. Signals from the cell's environment, including chemicals released by neighbouring cells and the cell's position in the developing organism, switch particular genes on or off. The same genome therefore produces different cell types depending on the environment each cell experiences.
items.specStatementText: Cells specialize by expressing different genes
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does differentiation involve changes to the DNA sequence?
items.correct: No. The DNA sequence is unchanged; differentiation involves changes in which genes are expressed.
items.misconception: Different cell types have accumulated different mutations, and these changes in the DNA sequence make the cells different.
items.why: Students learn that a change in phenotype is caused by a change in DNA, and the only mechanism for changing DNA they have met is mutation. Differentiation does not depend on mutation; the DNA sequence in a muscle cell and a neurone from the same organism is the same. What differs is the pattern of gene expression, controlled by regulatory proteins and by chemical modification of DNA and histones that do not alter the base sequence. Mutations are random and would not produce the reliable, organized development of tissues seen in every individual of a species.

items.q: Are unicellular eukaryotes an incomplete stage on the way to becoming multicellular?
items.correct: No. Unicellular eukaryotes are successful organisms in their own right, and most eukaryotic lineages have remained unicellular; multicellularity evolved in some lineages because it was advantageous there.
items.misconception: Unicellular organisms are primitive, transitional forms that will become multicellular given enough time, because multicellularity is more advanced.
items.why: Evolution is often pictured as a ladder of progress from simple to complex, and multicellular organisms are the ones students are most familiar with. Evolution has no goal. Unicellular eukaryotes are enormously abundant and diverse, and they have persisted alongside multicellular organisms for over a billion years. Multicellularity evolved repeatedly in lineages where a larger body and specialized cells gave an advantage, but in many environments a single cell that reproduces rapidly is at least as successful.
items.specStatementText: Multicellularity evolved many times and brings two advantages

items.q: Why does a larger body require many cells rather than one very large cell?
items.correct: Because as a cell grows its surface area to volume ratio falls, so a single very large cell could not exchange materials fast enough; many small cells keep an adequate ratio while the organism grows large.
items.misconception: A larger body could be achieved just as well by a single cell growing larger, so the only real advantage of multicellularity is cell specialization.
items.why: Students have met some very large single cells, such as egg cells, and body size is pictured as simply scaling everything up. Exchange of substances happens across the cell surface, but the demand for exchange depends on the cell's volume. As a cell gets larger its surface area to volume ratio falls, so a single cell cannot grow beyond a certain size and remain active. A multicellular organism keeps its cells small while its body becomes large, and can also specialize its cells, so multicellularity has both advantages: larger body size and cell specialization.
